newsitem.title: USA: NYS senator links gifts and underwriting awards.
newsitem.headline: NYS senator links gifts and underwriting awards.

text.p: The New York State Pataki Administration was attacked by a Democrat State Senator Wednesday for benefitting from big donations made by municipal bond underwriters who won profitable contracts.

Sen. Franz Leichter, D-Manhattan, said that state Republicans and local committees got almost $1 million in campaign contributions in 1995 and 1996. The firms that made the contributions were selected as underwriters for 248 municipal bond sales in the fourth quarter of 1996.

"It seems that there is not a campaign limitation or restriction that the state GOP does not try to evade or escape. The Republicans are greater escape artists than Houdini," said Leichter in prepared remarks.

He accused state Republicans of violating the spirit, if not the letter, of Securities and Exchange Commission rule G-37, which he said prohibits firms from making donations to state officials within two years of winning any negotiated municipal securities business in the state.
The federal Securities and Exchange Commission said it was taking "under consideration" the state senator's allegations that the contributions evaded Washington's ban on pay-to-play.
Gov. George Pataki said that bans restricting underwriting officials from making campaign contributions to back their beliefs were unfortunate.
A Pataki spokesman said that the state's selection of bond underwriters would not be swayed by the big donations that Leichter identified.

The Pataki Administration, which was bashed last year for benefiting in public opinion polls from advertisements run by committees promoting a $1.75 billion green bond, saw the issue flare up again. Two bond act committees, which Leichter said were controlled by Pataki and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, both Republicans, got nearly $300,000 from 13 underwriters.
Some of the bond underwriters that were identified by the state senator either declined comment or were not immediately available.

A spokeswoman for Prudential Securities said: "I can confirm the amount," explaining Leichter provided an aggregate sum. The state senator said Prudential gave $55,000 to the National Republican Senatorial Committee, and $500 to the Clean Air/Clean Water Bond Act Committee.

Undercutting Leichter's allegations that the contributions to state Republicans helped the firm win underwriting business, the Prudential spokeswoman added: "We gave substantially the same number to Democrats."

Others underwriters, like Smith Barney said only that they had made contributions to various Republican committees in 1995 and 1996. The firm gave $25,000 to the National Republican Senatorial Committee, and $25,000 to the Clean Air/Clean Water Bond Act Committee, Leichter said.

First Albany Corp denied an allegation by Leichter that its chief executive officer, George McNamee, had given $3,000 to a campaign for State Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, apparantly in violation of rule G-37.
"We always comply with G-37. We complied in this case and we reported contributions to the Municipal Securities Rule-Making Board as required," said Stephan Wink, general counsel for First Albany.

A source close to the firm, who declined to be identified, added that Leichter appeared to have double-counted some of the data. Leichter said the firm gave $25,000 to the Clean Air/Clean Water Bond Act Committee, $10,000 to the New York State Republican State Committee (housekeeping account), and $1,000 to the New York State Senate Republican Campaign Committee.

One underwriter, who declined to be identified, provided a copy of a solicitation from one of the green bond committees, the Clean Water/Clean Air Bond Act Committee, that said it was a nonpartisan body.
"The committee is not connected or affiliated with any political committees supporting Gov George Pataki or the New York Republican Party," the material said.
The committee was headed by the governor's counsel, who took a leave of absence to carry out the job.
